Secondary_Symptoms: Decreased range of motion in shoulder

patient_actor_hidden.Past_Medical_History: Diabetes mellitus type II, obesity, hypertension. On metformin, insulin, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide.
patient_actor_hidden.Social_History: Sedentary lifestyle, predominately staying indoors and watching television.

objective_for_doctor: Assess and diagnose the patient presenting with stiffness in his arm impacting daily activities.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

“I’ve been having stiffness in my arm for the past few months, and it’s made it hard to comb my hair and reach high shelves. I also notice my shoulder range of motion is decreased, and my arm feels a bit weaker.”
Can you tell me if the stiffness and weakness are limited to one shoulder/arm, or do you have similar symptoms in the other arm or elsewhere?
“It’s mainly in my left arm and shoulder—the other arm feels mostly normal. I don’t have stiffness or weakness anywhere else, and I haven’t noticed symptoms in other joints.”
Do you experience any pain in the left shoulder or arm? If so, can you describe where the pain is located, when it started, and what makes it better or worse.

“It’s not really sharp pain, more stiffness and a dull ache around the left shoulder and upper arm. It started gradually a few months ago and feels worse when I try to lift my arm overhead or reach up, and it’s a bit better when I rest.”
Do you notice any worsening of the stiffness or dull ache at night, especially when you lie on that side, and does it interfere with your sleep?
“It does seem a bit worse at night when I lie on my left side, and I’ve had some trouble sleeping because of the discomfort. When I change positions and rest my arm, it improves somewhat.”
Have you had any recent injuries, falls, or over‑use activities (e.g., heavy lifting, sports, repetitive motions) involving your left shoulder or arm?

“I haven’t had any injuries or falls, and I don’t do heavy lifting or sports. I’ve been mostly sedentary indoors and watching TV, with no specific repetitive shoulder use that started around the same time.”
Do you experience any numbness, tingling, or weakness that radiates down your left arm into the hand or fingers?
“No, I don’t have numbness or tingling, and the weakness feels more like a general loss of strength in the left arm rather than anything traveling down into my hand or fingers.”
May I ask how old you are and whether you have any medical conditions such as diabetes, thyroid disease, rheumatoid arthritis, or recent infections?
“I’m 65 years old. I have type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and I’m also obese, and I take metformin, insulin, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide.”
When a clinician moves your shoulder for you (passive motion), is the range of motion as limited as when you move it yourself (active motion), or is it noticeably better?

“It’s better when you move it for me—my active range of motion is more limited, especially lifting my arm overhead, but passive movement seems less restricted. I still feel that dull ache with overhead reaching, but it isn’t as tight when I’m not doing the lifting myself.”
[DDX] Rotator cuff tendinopathy/tear, Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder), Subacromial bursitis, Glenohumer
